image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   - **Bubble scatter plot**: circles plotted by year and earthquake magnitude, with circle size representing estimated deaths.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Single-panel chart** (no faceting or small multiples)
   - **Overplotted scatter/bubble marks**
   - **Size encoding** used for deaths
   - **Text annotations/labels** for selected earthquakes
   - One highlighted bubble uses a **dashed outline**

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year / date of earthquake | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Magnitude | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Estimated deaths | Quantitative | Circle area/size |
| Earthquake event / location-year label (e.g., Turkey, 1939; Armenia, 1988) | Categorical/nominal | Text label/annotation |
| Highlighted/annotated status for selected events | Categorical/nominal | Larger emphasized circles, annotation text, and in one case dashed outline |

Being someone who is interested in science, I find this graph fascinating. This graph shows multiple trends that may hint at many things. As time goes on in the graph, there are more earthquakes of lesser magnitude. There are also fewer earthquakes above a magnitude of 7 in the last 40 years. That being said, recent earthquakes seem to have more potential for high death tolls. The question for these trends is, why? 
First, the higher death tolls could be attributed to higher population, going from 20 million in 1950, to 80 million in 2020. This would lead to higher death tolls due to higher population density. 
Secondly, why are there an increase in the number of small earthquakes? I believe this could be attributed to an increase in technology of the region. Before 1960, seismometers may have just not been sensitive enough to detect an earthquake with a magnitude smaller than 5. However, there is also a trend for a decrease in high magnitude earthquakes. It appears that in the last 120 years, there have been a trend for smaller, more frequent earthquakes in turkey, indicating more frequent releases of energy in the crust. In my opinion, this graph shows how many documents can give more insight than what is obvious at a glance.

The graph is very telling of the hardships and losses Turkey and Syria have faced due to all these earthquakes. Perhaps my community could help keep people there safe in future earthquakes now that we know how prone this area is to large earthquakes. I would call this graph Shaken to the Core: Deaths from Major Earthquakes in Turkey and Northern Syria.

comments.raw_comment:
Turkey, Syria, and other countries in the Middle East sit on the Anatolian fault line, which is notorious for causing infrequent but strong tremors. This, paired with the high population density, and large amounts of impoverished people living in slums with unstable structures, especially near the Syrian border due to a large number of refugees, which creates a ticking time bomb.  This can be seen by the fact that all the high-magnitude earthquakes with high death tolls are located in the Middle East. This is also interesting to note how, despite these countries may not have the highest magnitude (namely the 1988 Armenian quake) but have disproportionally larger death tolls than other quakes of that magnitude. 
I wonder where the high magnitude quakes with low death tolls are centered. I hypothesize around the center of Turkey where there is less population density. 
This directly affects the community of people I interact with because I have a close friend who lives in Turkey who, thankfully, neither she nor her family was hurt, but her dad did lose his source of income because the building he worked in was destroyed. Turkey's government needs to be more prepared with better infrastructure in these high-population-density cities and a plan of action for immediate relief and recovery after a disaster like this. 
Title: Why does the Middle East Have Such high Death Tolls in Earthquakes?

comments.raw_comment: This graph demonstrates the amount and deaths of major earthquakes over the past 120 plus years around Turkey and Syria.  This directly connects to the recent earthquake in these areas from early February.  The main thing that stands out to me is how there is a very large frequency of earthquakes in this area.  Another thing that stands out is how certain earthquakes of larger magnitudes occasionally have lower death rates than certain ones, like the 1988 one in Armenia, for example.  This is quite interesting because one would assume quakes with larger magnitudes would have the most deaths.  I wonder what the reasoning behind these seemingly inconsistencies are.  Are the areas more or less populated?  Were people a bit more prepared?  Did rescue teams have a quicker strategy to help people?  This relates to me and my community because it is important to be prepared for all types of natural disasters and also raise awareness for those who recently experienced one.  I would entitle this graph: "Size vs. Deaths From Earthquakes."

I noticed that on this graph there have been 3 major earthquakes that happened in Turkey and in Syria in the years 1940, 2000, and then in the most recent year 2023 which is the one with the highest magnitude yet (7.8 magnitude).  Another major earthquake occurred in Armenia, 1988 with a magnitude of 6.8, but a mass amount of deaths (about 25,000+) which is more deaths than the most recent earthquake in 2023.

I wonder how the earthquake in Armenia had a lower magnitude than the most recent earthquake in Turkey and Syria, but still be able to cause more deaths than the earthquake in   Turkey and Syria that had a magnitude of 7.8 and Armenia had a magnitude of 6.8. I wonder what has been causing these earthquakes in these locations to have such a high magnitude in their earthquakes.
How does this relate to you and your community?

1) I noticed that from 1900 to 2023 the magnitude of the earthquake fluctuated years. From 1960 to 2023, more earthquakes have been occurring with magnitudes of all ranges from 4 to 7.8. comments.raw_comment:
1.  The most hazardous earthquakes, according to my observation, occurred in Turkey, Armenia, and Syria, with Turkey having an incredible three main quakes with magnitudes above 7. I also notice that there have been more earthquakes recently, with the number of earthquakes doubling after 1960 when they went from being very strong to being moderately weak. Since some earthquakes with magnitudes close to 8 have hardly any fatalities, the graph disproves the common belief that the higher the magnitude, the more deaths.

2. First, I'm curious as to why there have been twice as many earthquakes since 1960. Is this a result of rising populations or unstable building designs that have been made taller in many parts of the world? A change in our environment and the Earth's composition, which makes it simpler for these occurrences to recur, could also be blamed for the rise in smaller earthquakes below the magnitude of 5.

3. In New Jersey, I have never experienced an earthquake, and they are not at all common in this region. However, I believe that in the event of an earthquake, the number of fatalities would be relatively low given the lack of tall buildings in the area where I live. Unlike our neighboring state New York, where a single building collapsing could result in a significant number of fatalities.

4.  "The Effect of Earth's Deadliest Temper Tantrums"

What do you notice? 
I noticed that there have been various earthquakes around Turkey throughout the years from 1900-2023. While they've changed in size over the years, the earthquakes with the largest magnitudes are marked, the one Turkey and Syria in 2023 being the largest. There have been an estimate of about 20,000 deaths already and they're still increasing. There hasn't been an earthquake this large since 1939 in Turkey.

I wonder what has caused the amount of earthquakes occurring to increase. I also wonder if Turkey and other countries struggling with earthquakes have been able to prepare due to the fact that they've been happening for years.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because if an earthquake were ever to occur, we can try to prepare for it as best as we can. While they don't happen often in our community, it is always best to be prepared, especially with the previous knowledge we already have on earthquakes. We can also try to help others feel safe and prepared by helping out with donations and raising awareness of those struggling.

What do you notice?
In the graph I notice that the recent earthquake in Turkey & Syria has a record-breaking magnitude landing at 7.8, beating Turkey's worst earthquake in 1939 with a 7.7 magnitude and 32,000+ deaths. The last thing I noticed was that deadly earthquakes were getting more frequent; in the span of 40 years from 1900-1940, there was one major earthquake. Yet from 1980-2023, there have been 3 significant earthquakes. They seem to be progressively getting more frequent and violent. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what it is about Turkey and Syria's geography that makes them so prone to such extreme earthquakes. Multiple locations around the world seem to be more vulnerable to extreme earthquakes than others; could it be the long-lasting effects of climate change? I also wonder why although the magnitude of the 2023 earthquake was higher than the magnitude of the 1939 earthquake, the older one takes a death toll of 12,000 more people. 

How does this relate to my community and me?
This relates to me and my community because as we can see from the graph the rate of earthquake intensity is rising as the years increase, this means that natural disasters everywhere like hurricanes could increase in areas near me. Living near a bay puts my community at a higher risk for water natural disasters.

1. It is unfortunate to see that some of the worst earthquakes occur in Turkey. The 1940 Erzincan earthquake and the 1999 Ismit earthquake were both terrible, and this earthquake taking place now is approaching their death tolls.

I don’t want my demise to be located under piles of debris, so this makes me think of my own carbon footprint and my impact on the future of the planet I call home.
4. For a graph title, I would go between “All Shook Up” or “It’s Our ‘Fault’ ”

Turkey Earthquakes: Why are so many people still dying?
I notice that the higher the magnitude earthquake in Turkey, the higher the number of people who died rises as well. For example, in 1999 the 7.6 magnitude earthquake had roughly 17000 people die whereas in 2023 the 7.8 magnitude earthquake had roughly 20000 people die. I wonder why there was an anomaly in 1988 where the 6.8 magnitude earthquake had roughly 25000 people die. I just find it interesting that this specific earthquake had killed so many more people than the 7.6 magnitude earthquake and the 7.8 magnitude one. Also, I am curious as to why, with the more modern technology, so many more people had passed in more recent years. Yes, an earthquake can kill many, but I'm surprised with better technology and earlier warnings, how more people didn't try to get to better grounds, etc. This relates to my community and I because where I am from, the west side of Washington, there are many active volcanoes in our area. The Mount Saint Helen's eruption had killed many in 1980 and Mount Rainier is said to be long overdue for its eruption. In this graph you can see the different sized circles on a graph with years from 1900 on where they mark how many people died in a specific earthquake.
